newsitem.title: GERMANY: German neo-Nazis seen defying ban on Hess marches.
newsitem.headline: German neo-Nazis seen defying ban on Hess marches.

text.p: Tens of thousands of police across Germany have been put on standby to stop illegal marches this weekend by neo-Nazis to mark the 10th anniversary of the death of Hitler's deputy Rudolf Hess.
Police chiefs said they expected rallies to go ahead despite bans on assembly that have been issued by regional authorities across much of the country.
"There is also likely to be one main gathering," Erwin Hetger, head of police in the southern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg, said on ZDF television.

Hess hanged himself with an electric cord in Berlin's Spandau prison on August 17, 1987, and the date has become a rallying point for the radical right in Germany and other European countries in recent years.

Last year German police detained 160 right-wing activists on the ninth anniversary, while hundreds of neo-Nazis battled with police in Sweden, Norway and Germany's neighbour Denmark, which permits such rallies.

Danish police are this year yet again bracing for clashes between neo-Nazi groups from across Europe and leftist demonstrators, particularly in the normally quiet cathedral town of Roskilde, where a demonstration has been approved.

In Germany, Hess's anniversary provides the occasion for much public soul-searching about the continued presence of right-wing thuggery and the appeal of Nazism within a country still acutely aware of its past.

The recent surge in joblessness to levels not seen since Adolf Hitler's rise to power in the early 1930s has, at a time when Germany has been the recipient of new waves of immigrants from eastern Europe, this year added to the concern.

But Klaus Hardrath, Interior Minister for Saxony, one of the eastern states that since unification has been a focus of neo-Nazi violence, said today's hard-right extremists were primarily young, but not always poor and disaffected.

"The drift into right-wing extremism is not to do with unemployment or the lack of training places -- the vast majority of those under suspicion have got a training place or are still at school," Hardrath told Berlin radio.
Presenting 1996 data on far-right criminality in Saxony, Hardrath said violence with a clear right-wing motivation in 40 percent of cases followed the drinking of alcohol.
Around a third of such incidents happened in or outside bars or discos, he said, adding nearly half of those charged already had a record of violence without any discernible far-right motivation.
"(The far-right scene) is very unorganised, not particularly political and very theoretical," agreed Green Party politician Krista Sager, speaking on regional southern German radio.

For many of those attracted to far-right ideology and its accompanying legends, Hess, the private secretary to whom Hitler dictated his political testament Mein Kampf, has achieved the status of martyr.

Appointed deputy Fuehrer in 1932, he was effectively in charge of the Nazi party until 1941, when he parachuted into Scotland on a mysterious mission to press for an Anglo-German alliance against the Soviet Union.
He spent the rest of his life in custody, the last two decades as the sole inmate of Spandau, where many extremists claim he was murdered by the Allies.
